newsitem.title: USA: Confident Clinton in hectic election eve push.
newsitem.headline: Confident Clinton in hectic election eve push.

text.p: An exuberant President Bill Clinton on Monday raced the clock to Tuesday's election with a final campaign blitz that blended sentimentality with hard-nosed political calculations.

Arriving here in the wee hours of the morning after a lively post-midnight rally in Maine, Clinton grabbed about three hours of sleep, then held a reunion with old friends and supporters at Merrimack Restaurant, where he often ate breakfast during the 1992 New Hampshire primary campaign.

Clinton's eyes filled with tears as he greeted Michael Morrison, a wheelchair-bound New Hampshire teenager who helped put him on the road to the White House four years ago. Stooping to hug Morrison, the president said: "This election day, you won't have to push that wheelchair."
Later, in a speech to a crowd huddled in bone-chilling weather outside the restaurant, Clinton said New Hampshire and the country did not have to take a gamble on him, as was the case four years ago.

"You know that compared to four years ago, in terms of the economy, the lowest crime rate in 10 years, declining welfare rolls, rising child support collection, in almost every way of indicating the character of American life, we are moving forward," he said.
"Are we going to finish the job?" Clinton asked rhetorically. "Your vote will decide."
He repeated a folksy assurance he gave New Hampshire voters in 1992 -- that he would be with them "till the last dog dies" -- and added: "Well folks, there's a lot of life left in this old dog."

The main event on Clinton's election eve schedule was a noontime rally in Cleveland with Vice President Al Gore designed to counter a late surge in Ohio by Republican Bob Dole. Hillary Rodham Clinton and Tipper Gore were to join their husbands in campaigning there.

From Cleveland, Clinton was to hopscotch by air across the U.S. mid-section, stopping in Lexington, Kentucky, Des Moines, Iowa and Sioux Falls, South Dakota before flying home to Little Rock, Arkansas to vote on Tuesday.

The Clinton camp was confident the election would make him the first Democrat since Franklin Roosevelt in 1936 to win a second consecutive term and the mood aboard the president's plane was euphoric, like a winning team's locker room.

Clinton aides predicted he would defeat Dole in every one of the states on the final swing and said he was going to two of them -- Iowa and South Dakota -- only to help Democratic candid for the Senate.
Although polling conducted for Reuters shows Clinton's lead over Dole narrowing, his campaign officials insisted their extensive polling showed him with a steady 12- to 15-percentage-point lead.
They said the only question was whether Clinton would get a majority of the popular vote, improving on his 43 percent plurality in 1992 when he defeated then-President George Bush.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton had already set in motion a process to review potential staff changes if he is re-elected. He said Clinton would move quickly to reshape his team, including Cabinet officers.

Administration officials said there were no plans for a huge shakeup, although several key Clinton confidants, including six or more Cabinet officers, were expected to leave. White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta has said he plans to step down, perhaps to run for California governor.
